lanes.summary: Wild::AdminTools has the best-articulated safety architecture in the gem (allowlist -> param validation -> rate limit -> blast radius -> two-phase nonce -> audit -> gate) and its tool-boundary "safety" specs are genuinely adversarial, not vanity. But the primitive the whole design rests on is broken: NonceManager does check-then-act around a NonceStore that has no compare-and-set, so one single-use confirmation nonce double-consumes ~10% of the time under 8-way concurrency and executes a mutate_destructive action twice. Second, the namespace cannot actually be wired to a Rails app today: the three concrete adapters (RailsCache/Sidekiq/Flipper, 291 LOC) are never required so they raise NameError, the central Wild.config.admin_tools :default sentinels are read by nobody, and Configuration#validate! -- the only guard against nil adapters -- is never called, so the documented initializer silently yields "undefined method read_key for nil" on every action. Third, several controls are weaker than their names: AuditedPipeline publicly delegates a two_phase reader that executes destructive actions with zero audit/gate/rate-limit/blast-radius; the "opaque failure reason" nonce contract leaks internal_reason to the client; blast radius scores 16 of 19 actions as 1 (including enable_flag_percentage); and the policy "defaults" section is validated as required but never applied, so an action relying on it crashes the limiter with NoMethodError. None of these are unfixable -- most are one-to-ten-line fixes -- but as shipped this namespace is a well-drawn design that has never been run against a real Rails app.

confirmed.evidence: retention_manager.rb:45-56 `File.foreach(@store.path) do |line| ... end; File.write(@store.path, kept_lines.join)` operates on @store.path with no synchronization; json_lines_store.rb:16,22 shows @mutex is a private ivar on the JsonLinesStore instance, never passed to or shared with RetentionManager.

votes.reason: Verified by direct read: purge_before (retention_manager.rb:41-58) and remove_oldest_until_within_limit (60-73) do File.foreach/File.readlines then File.write on @store.path with zero synchronization. JsonLinesStore#append (json_lines_store.rb:20-26) is the only writer that takes @mutex, and @mutex is a private ivar never shared with RetentionManager. No flock/advisory locking exists anywhere in the store code (grep confirmed). A concurrent append landing between a purge's read and its File.write overwrite is built from a stale snapshot and the append is lost — real Ruby file-IO race, not a misreading of semantics. Matches facts.json verified_facts.retention-purge-outside-mutex verbatim and is tracked as still-open (wild-rvv.5.3 / MIN-Kleppmann), not in known_and_already_fixed, and not covered by any out_of_scope entry.

Both named files exist (test -f passes for lib/wild/telemetry/collector/store/retention_manager.rb and lib/wild/telemetry/collector/store/json_lines_store.rb). The literal repro runs (exit 0) and shows exactly what the claim says: purge_before (lines 41-58) does File.foreach(@store.path) then File.write(@store.path, kept_lines.join), and remove_oldest_until_within_limit (60-73) does File.readlines then File.write, with no synchronization; json_lines_store.rb:16 creates @mutex as a private instance ivar with no reader/accessor, and every JsonLinesStore method (append/recent/find/count/query/clear!/size_bytes) wraps in it, so the store's own lock is bypassed by RetentionManager. The only store method RetentionManager calls under the mutex is size_bytes (line 28), which does not cover the read-modify-write. No diff between base 339453f and HEAD 397c5e2 in lib/wild/telemetry/collector/store/. A concurrent Ruby repro (2000 appends racing 300 purge_expired calls on a seeded file) lost 425 of 2000 appended events, empirically confirming the lost-write race, not just the missing lock. Matches verified_facts 'retention-purge-outside-mutex' and open bead wild-rvv.5.3 (MIN-Kleppmann append-only framing). Not in known_and_already_fixed (PR #52 only fixed the time-bomb fixture in the retention spec, not the concurrency). The claim is technically accurate and the cited lines exist verbatim at the stated positions (verified identical at both base 339453f and current HEAD): retention_manager.rb:56 `File.write(@store.path, kept_lines.join)` in #purge_before and :71 `File.write(@store.path, lines.join)` in #remove_oldest_until_within_limit. Ruby's File.write opens in truncate mode ("w") by default, so a crash between open-truncate and write-completion does leave the target file blank or partially written — no temp-file+rename, no fsync anywhere in this class or in JsonLinesStore. No guard elsewhere neutralizes this: JsonLinesStore#append/#recent/#find/#count all synchronize on @mutex, but RetentionManager reads/writes @store.path directly and never touches that mutex (a related, separately-flagged concurrency gap), so nothing about the mutex protects against the crash scenario either. Not refuted on correctness grounds. However, reachability from any in-process public entry point (Gate#evaluate, Pipeline.process, ServerFactory.create, AuditedPipeline) is absent: grep across all of lib/ shows RetentionManager is `require`d only by collector.rb (a namespace/require-aggregator file with no methods) and is never `.new`'d anywhere in lib/ — its only instantiations in the whole repo are in three spec files (retention_manager_spec.rb, safety_rules_spec.rb, threat_mitigations_spec.rb). There is also no rake task, bin/, or scheduler wiring that invokes purge_expired/purge_oversized/purge_all. So today this is dead/unconsumed code: the crash-corruption scenario cannot occur in any running Wild deployment because nothing calls the purge path. Additionally this exact durability question is already an open, explicitly tracked decision bead in facts.json's council ledger: wild-rvv.5.3 "MIN-Kleppmann: Decide fsync per append OR drop append-only audit log framing from telemetry collector" (status Open, priority 1) — the same bead the finding itself cites under `related.beads`. Given true unreachability from any public entry point plus pre-existing tracking of the identical concern, I recommend downgrading from the reported P1 to P2 rather than dropping it outright (the code defect is real and will matter the moment Role 7/8 wires retention into a live scheduler).
